source_text: Sed ne nimis primam partem certaminis urgeamus, patiamur processu opinionis te bonam Adae probare naturam. Dicis profecto: Deus iustus legem devotionis homini non poneret, si eum nosset pati peccandi necessitatem; quia si iustitiam voluntatis exigeret ab eo quem malae naturae esse nosset, non illum cum praevaricabatur, reum arguebat, sed se inimicum esse iustitiae publicabat. Posuit autem Deus iustus legem homini, quem ulturum se, si fuisset praevaricatus, spopondit. Constat ergo eum bonum natura, non potuisse aliter, nisi sola voluntate peccare. Vides nempe, quam legitima sit a me tuo nomine prolata conclusio? Ipse est omnino gladius, qui in manu Catholicorum coruscans, Manichaeos Traducianosque populatur. Sed nimis propter vestrum nomen admiscui, quorum vice impraesentiarum volueram responsum videri. Concussit ergo Manichaeum solida responsio. Augustam rationem dignis laudibus prosequor: verum oleo laudationis huius, in te acui gladium contuere. Repete igitur, quaeso, quod dixeras. Deus iustus, inquis, legem non poneret homini, si esset malum natura; posuit autem legem qui iustus est; apparet nunc potuisse servare, quod aequissimus imperavit; quoniam nisi obediendi virtutem habuisset, numquam constaret praecipienti ratio iussionis. O lepidissimum capitulum! Me coram, me spectatore, bonitatem naturae, cui lex ponitur, de iustitia legem promulgantis affirmat; nec videt se, antequam vulnusculum Manichaeus sentiat, in Traducianos exitium pertulisse. Ut enim intellegas semineci me tibi rapere arma cruenta, victricemque ferant morientia lumina veritatem [n70] , in tua temet tela compellam. Si iustus Deus Adae legem dare non potuit, nisi eum sciret sine aliquo mali coactu liberum posse observare quod iustum est; sine dubio et in temporibus secutis eadem gravitate iustitiae lex etiam litteris tradita, multiplicatione diffusior, distinctione signatior, et aucta ultione reverentior, data hominibus non fuisset, si aut imbecilli ad faciendum bonum sine possibilitate iustitiae, aut rei, id est mali, ab utero nascerentur; quoniam ut istos in omni praevaricatione necessitatis excusaret obtentus; ita immoderatio praeceptorum, impotentia sanctionum, iniquitas iudiciorum, in maculam rediret auctoris. Igitur et haec pars secunda eodem genere, quo prior, cluditur; id est, ut confitearis, aut iustitiam Dei non potuisse imperare, nisi quod a subditis fieri posse perpenderet; et testimonio primi mandati Manichaeus, testimonio autem legum postea secutarum Manichaeus Traducianusque consumitur; aut si hoc relinquit impietas, ne leviter quidem a vobis pulsatus Manichaeus, vestrum se esse patrem, vestrum principem, cumque vobis adversum nos unicum sibi esse certamen, mundo teste monstrabit.
pass_a_gloss: But lest we press the first part of the contest too much, let us suffer you by the progress of opinion to prove Adam's nature good. You say indeed: A just God would not place a law of devotion on a human, if he knew him to suffer a necessity of sinning; because if he demanded a justice of will from him whom he knew to be of an evil nature, he was not accusing him guilty when he was prevaricating, but was publishing himself an enemy of justice. But a just God placed a law on the human, whom he pledged he would avenge, if he had prevaricated. It stands therefore that he good by nature could not otherwise sin except by will alone. You perceive indeed how legitimate the conclusion brought forth by me in your name is? He is altogether the sword which flashing in the Catholics' hand lays waste Manichaeans and Traducians. But I mixed too much on account of your name, in whose turn I had wanted a reply to seem for the present. A solid reply therefore shook Manichaeus. I follow a narrow reason with worthy praises: but by the oil of this praise, look that a sword is sharpened against you. Repeat therefore, I ask, what you had said. A just God, you say, would not place a law on a human, if evil were by nature; but he who is just placed a law; it appears now that he could keep what the most equitable commanded; because unless he had had a virtue of obeying, the reason of the command would never stand for the one precepting. O most charming little chapter! In my presence, with me as spectator, he affirms the goodness of nature, on which a law is placed, from the justice of the one promulgating the law; nor does he see that, before Manichaeus feels a little wound, he has brought destruction upon the Traducians. For that you may understand that I snatch from you half-dead the bloody arms, and that dying lights may bear conquering truth, I will compel you into your own weapons. If a just God could not give a law to Adam, unless he knew him free without some co-forcing of evil able to observe what is just; without doubt also in following times by the same gravity of justice a law also handed over in letters, more diffuse by multiplication, more marked by distinction, and more reverent by increased vengeance, would not have been given to humans, if they were born either weak for doing good without a possibility of justice, or guilty, that is evil, from the womb; because as a pretext of necessity would excuse these in every prevarication; so an immoderation of precepts, an impotence of sanctions, an iniquity of judgments, would return into a stain of the author. Therefore this second part also is closed by the same kind as the earlier; that is, that you confess either that the justice of God could not command except what it weighed could be done by subjects; and by the testimony of the first mandate Manichaeus, but by the testimony of the laws following afterward Manichaeus and the Traducian is consumed; or if impiety leaves this, Manichaeus not even lightly struck by you will show, the world being witness, that he is your father, your prince, and that with you against us there is a unique contest for himself.

pass_b_english: But let us not press the first part of the contest too hard. Let us allow you to proceed in your opinion and prove Adam’s nature good. You surely say: A just God would not impose a law of devotion on a human being if he knew that person suffered a necessity of sinning. If he demanded justice of will from someone he knew to possess an evil nature, he would not prove the transgressor guilty, but publicly show himself an enemy of justice. Yet the just God imposed a law on humanity and promised punishment for transgression. It is therefore established that the human being, good by nature, could sin only by will alone.

You see how sound a conclusion I have offered in your name? It is precisely the sword that flashes in catholic hands and lays waste both Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin. But I too quickly brought in your party’s name, though for now I wanted my reply taken as yours. The solid response has therefore shaken Mani. I accompany this august reasoning with fitting praise, but notice that the oil of this praise sharpens the sword against you.

Repeat, please, what you said. ‘The just God would not impose a law on humanity if it were evil by nature. But he, being just, imposed a law. It is now clear that humanity could keep what the perfectly fair God commanded, because without the power to obey, the one commanding could never have a reasonable basis for his order.’ What a delightful little argument! Before me, with me as spectator, he establishes the goodness of the nature receiving law from the justice of the lawgiver—and does not see that before Mani feels even a small wound, he has brought destruction upon the advocates of inherited sin.

To make you understand that I seize your bloody weapons while you lie half-dead, and that your dying eyes must bear the sight of victorious truth, I will drive you onto your own weapons. [Literary echo: Virgil, Aeneid 10.462–463.] If the just God could not give Adam a law unless he knew him free to observe justice without any compulsion toward evil, then without doubt the law of later times, carrying the same weight of justice, could not have been given to people if they were born from the womb either weak for good and incapable of justice, or guilty—that is, evil. That later law was also put in writing, more extensive through multiplied provisions, more precise through distinctions, and more fearsome through increased punishment.

For just as the plea of necessity would excuse these people in every transgression, the excessive commands, uncontrolled decrees, and unjust judgments would return as a stain upon their author. Thus this second part closes in the same way as the first. Either you acknowledge that God’s justice could command only what he judged those subject to him could do—in which case the first command destroys Mani, while the later laws destroy Mani and the advocate of inherited sin together—or, if impiety abandons this argument, Mani has not suffered even a slight blow from you. With the world as witness, he will show that he is your father and leader, and that he and you have one single contest against us.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
